title: Add an agent written in code

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A **code agent** is a Python program that runs under the same guarantees as any agent: the runner starts
  it, decides its permissions, counts its turns, journals its tool calls and reads its result. Use it for a
  program of your own that must run governed. A fixed computation with no model is a `job`; a judgement
  that instructions can carry is a prompt agent.
- Two people are involved: the author, who builds the image, and the **operator**, who names it. A workflow
  or an agent never writes an image.
- Read `docs/code-agents.md`: this page is its checklist.

sections.title: At the registry
sections.markdown:
1. Write the agent with `choregos-agent-sdk`: `@agent(name=...)`, an `async def run(ctx)` that uses
   `ctx.llm` for the model and `ctx.tools()` for tools, and returns a `Result`.
2. Build the image **FROM the runner image**: the runner is the entrypoint and your agent is the
   subprocess it starts. Give the agent its own virtualenv. See `examples/agents/plain/Dockerfile`.
3. Check it with `make conformance-agent IMAGE=<reference> COMMAND='[...]'`, then push the image and
   note its **digest**.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- The model is reached only through the gateway, with the run's own key. No provider key is in the pod.
- `tools.call` and `write_output` ask the runner's guard first. Calling a tool server or a provider
  directly works and **skips the guard**: no permission request, no journal line, no turn count.
- The sandbox (RuntimeClass, network policy, egress proxy) bounds what your code reaches.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. **The operator names the image**: `global.images.agents` in the chart maps a name to a reference
   **pinned by digest**. By default (`global.images.requireDigest: true`) a tag-only reference stops the API and
   the workers at start-up; `false` is for a bench only.
2. **Agents**, **New**, **Runtime**: choose **Code (image)**. Pick the image by its name, give the command
   (one argument per line) and the model API (`openai` or `anthropic`).
3. Run it from a workflow like any registry agent. Use an executor that starts a pod per run
   (`k8s_job`): `agent_sandbox` runs one pool image and refuses a run whose image differs.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Run the conformance suite on the image, then run a one-step workflow with the agent and read its journal
and its result.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- An unknown image name is refused at publication, and the error lists the known names: the operator has
  not named it yet.
- The API or the workers stop at start-up naming a tag-only reference: pin the image by digest.
- `agent_sandbox` refuses the image: the pool was made from another one; use `k8s_job`.
- The run ends `max_turns`, or `permission_denied`: the guard stopped it, by design.
- `agent_error`: your function raised; the journal has the traceback line.

egress: the registry that holds the agent image

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
ChatGPT connects **to** Choregos through the MCP door, with **your** rights and never more. It lists your
projects, reads workflows and work items, and tells you what waits for a decision. It never decides: a
decision needs you, signed in again, in the console. The door is `https://choregos.example.com/mcp`.

ChatGPT calls from the vendor's cloud and signs in with OAuth, so it needs a public HTTPS address and OAuth enabled on the door.

sections.title: At the client
sections.markdown:
The Integrations page of this console is the procedure: it gives the exact snippet for ChatGPT, with this
platform's address filled in. Open it with the link below the panel.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
OAuth: your identity provider's token, with the `mcp:read` or `mcp:write` scope it granted, then your role. The door refuses a full-access token. A token can be bound to one project, and the door's tools
announce only what your role allows.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown: Open **Integrations**, choose ChatGPT and copy the snippet. The page gives what to enter when the platform names a ChatGPT client.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Ask the client "what is waiting for my decision in Choregos?". It should call `list_pending_decisions`.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401`: the token is missing, unknown, revoked or expired.
- `403 insufficient_scope`: a full-access token was used; mint an `mcp:read` or `mcp:write` one.
- A tool is missing: a read-only token, a role without the right, or a project whose tracker is external.
- The connector cannot be reached: the platform has no public HTTPS address, or it is behind a VPN.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A **remote agent** runs elsewhere: a workflow step calls it over the A2A protocol and takes its answer
  as the step's result. It is the reverse of the MCP door. Choregos reads its **card** and pins it.
- You need the **agent card URL** (A2A 0.3 serves `/.well-known/agent.json`; newer versions an
  `agent-card.json`), the protocol version it speaks, the **skill** to call and how it authenticates.
- An organisation administrator does the first part (the credential); whoever builds agents does the
  second.
- The agent acts with whatever identity the credential carries. Choose that account with care.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown:
1. In the vendor's administration, allow the agent to be called by other applications, if it asks for it.
2. Note the card URL. If it uses OAuth and its card advertises **dynamic client registration**, you
   register nothing. Otherwise register a client at the vendor with the redirect address below and keep
   its client id and secret.
3. Authentication is one of: OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE; a bearer token; or none.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- The credential decides what the agent may do. Prefer a dedicated account holding only the access the
  agent needs.
- OAuth redirect (callback) address to register, when the vendor needs one: `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/remote-credentials/oauth/callback`.
- The refresh token is sealed in the platform's secret store and never shown again; reconnecting replaces
  it.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Remote agents**, **Connect**: give the card URL, then sign in **as the account the
   agent will act as** and accept. The credential shows `connected` and who it is authorised as.
2. **Agents**, **New**, **Remote agent (A2A)**: paste the card URL, **Read the card**, pick the skill and
   the credential, set the timeout and the **declared cost** (A2A reports none: it is declared, not
   measured), then publish. Publication pins the card's digest.
3. Allow the hosts: a project that uses it must allow the agent's host in `sandbox.network.allow_domains`,
   and the runner pods, the API and the orchestrator must be allowed to reach the card, endpoint and
   token hosts (see the network allowlist of your platform).

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Add a two-step workflow: the remote agent, then a human review of its answer. The answer is
`response.md`, an artifact of the step; the facts it states are recorded as declared, never measured.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `remote_card_changed`: the card changed since publication. Publish a new version to accept it.
- `remote_auth_required`: the credential expired or was revoked. Reconnect it.
- `remote_input_required`: the agent asked a question. It is shown; answering it from the console is not
  supported yet.
- `remote_timeout`: the remote task is cancelled; raise the timeout or narrow the task.
- A cut at about 30 s on a synchronous call: Choregos streams, so a long task still works.
- A refusal naming a host: it is not in the stage's allowed domains, or the platform's egress allowlist
  does not open it.

title: Add Atlassian Rovo as a remote agent

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- An Atlassian site with **Rovo**, and an Atlassian organisation administrator.
- A **dedicated Atlassian account** (for example `choregos-bot@your-domain`) licensed for Rovo, whose Jira
  and Confluence permissions are exactly what Rovo may do for Choregos. Rovo acts **as that user**. There
  are no service accounts for A2A.
- This calls the Rovo **agent**. To give your own agents Rovo's **tools** (search, Jira, Confluence) use
  the Rovo MCP Server procedure instead; they are two different things.
- Not run against the real service from this repository: the registration exchange with Atlassian is
  exercised against a fake. Check the first connection on a test site.

sections.title: At Atlassian
sections.markdown:
1. In Atlassian Administration, **allow A2A connections** (Manage A2A connections in Admin Hub).
2. The agent card is `https://a2a.atlassian.com/.well-known/agent.json` and the endpoint
   `https://a2a.atlassian.com/v1/rovo`, A2A 0.3.0. It is **one agent with two skills**:
   `work-in-jira` and `work-in-confluence`. Agents built in Rovo Studio are **not** individually
   addressable.
3. You register no client: the card advertises dynamic client registration and Choregos registers itself.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE and dynamic client registration, nothing else: no API token.
  Scopes: `read:me`, `offline_access`, `full_access:chat:rovo`.
- The callback address Choregos registers is `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/remote-credentials/oauth/callback`.
- The agent can do whatever the dedicated account can do in Jira and Confluence.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Remote agents**, **Connect**: card URL `https://a2a.atlassian.com/.well-known/agent.json`.
   Atlassian's consent page opens: sign in **as the dedicated account** and accept. The credential shows
   `connected` and who it is authorised as.
2. **Agents**, **New**, **Remote agent (A2A)**: paste the same card URL, **Read the card**, pick the skill
   (`work-in-jira` or `work-in-confluence`) and the credential, and set the timeout.
3. Set the **declared cost**: Rovo reports none, and its use counts against your Atlassian subscription.
4. Allow `a2a.atlassian.com` in the projects that use it (`sandbox.network.allow_domains`), and open
   `a2a.atlassian.com` for the runner pods and `auth.atlassian.com` for the API and the orchestrator.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Add a two-step workflow: a step with the Rovo agent asking for a read-only summary of a Jira issue, then a
human review. The answer is the step's `response.md`.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `access_denied` at consent: A2A connections are not allowed in Atlassian Administration.
- `401` when the token is refreshed: it was revoked. Reconnect the credential.
- `remote_card_changed`: Atlassian changed the card. Publish a new version to accept it.
- A cut at about 30 s on a synchronous call: Choregos streams; Rovo has no push notifications.
- A refusal naming `a2a.atlassian.com` or `auth.atlassian.com`: the stage's allowed domains or the
  egress allowlist.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- Argo CD, and a **GitOps repository** it watches. Choregos never runs `kubectl apply`: a promotion is a
  pull request on that repository, and Argo CD applies it.
- The GitHub App of the platform installed on the GitOps repository (see the GitHub procedures): the
  writes go through it.
- The platform's shared webhook secret (`CHOREGOS_GENERIC_WEBHOOK_SECRET`).

sections.title: At Argo CD
sections.markdown:
1. Create a local account or use a project role for the platform, and generate an **API token** for it
   (`argocd account generate-token --account <name>`). Give it read access to the applications only.
2. Send application health events to `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/argocd` with the header `X-Choregos-Secret` set to
   the shared secret (an Argo CD Notifications webhook service does this).
3. Name applications by one pattern. The connector looks for `{app}-{env}` (for example `billing-prod`)
   unless `app_pattern` says otherwise.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- The API token: `get` on applications, nothing more. Writes never use it.
- The GitHub App: `contents` and `pull_requests` write on the GitOps repository.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Project settings, Connectors, **CD**, type **Argo CD**.
2. `gitops_repo`: `owner/repo`. `base_url`: the Argo CD server's address. `path_prefix` and `app_pattern`
   if your layout differs from `apps/` and `{app}-{env}`.
3. `token`: the API token, in the password field.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Press **Test**: it calls Argo CD's `/api/version` and shows the version. A promotion on a test
application then proves the GitOps write.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401` or `403` on the test: the token is wrong, expired, or the account has no `get` right.
- The pull request is not opened: the GitHub App is not installed on the GitOps repository, or lacks
  `pull_requests: write`.
- Health never changes on the work item: Argo CD's events do not reach the webhook, or the application's
  name does not follow `app_pattern`.

fields.gitops_repo: owner/repo of the GitOps repository the promotions are written to
fields.app_pattern: how an application is named, {app}-{env} by default
fields.path_prefix: the directory of the applications in the GitOps repository, apps by default
fields.token: an Argo CD API token, read only, typed once

- State that disappears: it lives in memory; with several replicas, set `url` to a single process.

fields.url: the endpoint of the one process serving the demonstration fakes; empty to run them in this process
fields.api_key: not needed by the demonstration, typed once if you set one

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A cluster where Tekton Pipelines is installed, and a namespace where the project's `PipelineRun`s run.
- The platform reads the cluster with the API's own in-cluster service account: it must be allowed to
  `get` and `list` `pipelineruns.tekton.dev` in that namespace. If you only use GitHub Actions, the
  project needs no `ci` connector: checks are read through the `scm` connector.
- The platform's shared webhook secret (`CHOREGOS_GENERIC_WEBHOOK_SECRET`).

sections.title: At the cluster
sections.markdown:
1. Label each `PipelineRun` the platform should follow with `choregos/sha=<commit>`; the connector
   finds a commit's runs through that label. Runs that carry `choregos/project`, `choregos/work-item`
   and `choregos/run-id` are also mapped back to their work item.
2. Point Tekton's CloudEvents sink at the platform:
   `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/tekton?jeton=<the shared webhook secret>`. Tekton's sink is configured by URL and
   cannot add a header, which is why the secret travels in the query string.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- A `Role` granting `get`, `list` on `pipelineruns` in the namespace, bound to the API's service account.
- The shared webhook secret is the only credential of the sink. Treat the URL as a secret.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Project settings, Connectors, **CI**, type **Tekton Pipelines**.
2. `namespace`: where the runs live. `pipeline`: the Pipeline's name, `choregos-ci` by default.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Press **Test**: the connector asks the cluster for the Tekton API and answers `ok`. Then start a build
and watch its state change on the work item.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `Forbidden` from the cluster: the API's service account lacks the `Role` above.
- Status stays `unknown`: no `PipelineRun` carries the `choregos/sha` label of that commit.
- Tekton events refused with `401`: the secret in the sink URL differs from the platform's.
- Events never arrive: the sink URL is unreachable from the cluster, or Tekton's `config-defaults` ConfigMap does
  not name it in `default-cloud-events-sink`.

fields.namespace: the namespace whose PipelineRuns carry the project's builds

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- An Atlassian administrator, for a **service account** (recommended) or a dedicated user.
- The Confluence space (and, if you want only a branch, the page) to read. The account's permissions are
  what Choregos can read: everything it reads in the space becomes readable by everyone the knowledge
  base is open to, whatever the page restrictions say for other people.

sections.title: At Atlassian
sections.markdown:
Two ways; the scoped one is recommended.

**Scoped token on a service account (recommended).** Atlassian Administration, Directory,
**Service accounts**: create one, then **Create credentials**, an **API token with scopes**. The expiry
is between 1 and 365 days: note it. Copy the token when it is shown.

**Classic token on a user account.** On `id.atlassian.com`, Security, **API tokens**, **Create API
token**. It carries all of that user's rights: prefer a Confluence-only user.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- Scopes for a scoped token: `read:space:confluence`, `read:page:confluence`,
  `read:hierarchical-content:confluence`, plus `read:attachment:confluence` when the source indexes
  attachments.
- Give the account **read** on the spaces to index (Space settings, Permissions) and nothing else.
- A scoped token is only accepted through `https://api.atlassian.com/ex/confluence/<cloudId>/…`, with
  Basic authentication using the service account's email. Choregos does that when `auth` is `scoped`.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Documents**, type **Confluence**.
2. `base_url`: `https://<site>.atlassian.net`. `email`: the account's email.
3. `auth`: `basic` (the default) for a classic token, `scoped` for a scoped one. For `scoped`, set
   `cloud_id`; the site publishes it at `https://<site>.atlassian.net/_edge/tenant_info`.
4. `api_token`: paste the token in the password field (sealed, shown once).
5. **Knowledge**, a base, **Add source**, **Confluence**: pick the connector, a space key (for example
   `ENG`; a personal space starts with `~`), optionally a page id (the number in
   `…/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/<id>/Title`) for that page and everything under it, labels, attachments.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Add the source and press **Sync now**: it lists the space once and downloads each page. A first sync
that adds documents proves the token, the scopes, `cloud_id` and the space permission.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401` with a scoped token: `auth` is still `basic`. A scoped token is refused on the site's own address.
- `401` with a classic token: wrong email, or a revoked token.
- `403`, or an empty space: the account has no read permission on that space, or a scope is missing.
- `404` on the space: the space key is case-sensitive.
- `429`: Atlassian's rate limit. The sync waits for `Retry-After` and tries again.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `api.atlassian.com` (scoped) or the site (classic).

fields.email: the email of the account the token belongs to (the service account's, for a scoped token)
fields.auth: basic for a classic token, scoped for a scoped token
fields.cloud_id: scoped tokens only: the site's cloud id

title: Connect a private git repository as a documents source

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A **private** git repository whose documentation (Markdown by default) a knowledge base should read. A
  public repository needs no connector: a git source reads it directly.
- This is an organisation connector: an organisation administrator declares it once. The credential is
  **pinned to its host**: a source whose repository is on another host is refused, so a token is never
  sent elsewhere. Declare one connector per host.

sections.title: At the forge
sections.markdown:
**Token (simplest).** GitHub: Settings, Developer settings, **Fine-grained personal access tokens**,
Generate new token. Pick **only the repository** and the repository permission **Contents: Read-only**.
Set an expiry and note it. The token is sent to git as HTTP Basic with the user name `x-access-token`; that
is what GitHub expects, and it has **not been verified here against other forges**, so test a GitLab or
Gitea host before relying on it.

**GitHub App (no token to rotate).** Create or reuse an App with the repository permission
**Contents: Read-only**, install it on the repository, and note its **App ID**, the **installation id**
(the number at the end of the installation's address) and a generated **private key**. At each read the
platform mints a one-hour installation token limited to that repository and to `contents: read`.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- Contents read on the one repository, nothing else. No write permission is needed or used.
- The credential travels to git in the environment, never on a command line, in an error message or in
  `.git/config`.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Documents**, type **Git over https**.
2. `host`: `github.com` (the default) or your host.
3. `auth`: `token`, then paste the token in `token`. Or `auth`: `github_app`, then `app_id`, optionally
   `installation_id`, and the App's key in `private_key`. For GitHub Enterprise Server also set `api_url`.
4. **Knowledge**, a base, **Add source**, kind **Git**: pick this connector, then the repository's https
   address, a `ref` (a branch is followed, a commit is pinned) and `paths` (globs; markdown by default).

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Add the source and press **Sync now**. A repository whose files match `paths` adds documents; a
repository where no file matches is reported unreadable and **deletes nothing**.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A refusal saying the address is not on the connector's host: the repository is on another host than
  the connector's `host`, by design.
- `Authentication failed` or `404` from git: the token is wrong, expired or has no access to that
  repository; for an App, it is not installed on the repository.
- "not an https address": a git source is fetched over https only.
- Unreadable, nothing deleted: no file matches `paths`, or the `ref` does not exist.
- A timeout: the git fetch is cut at 5 minutes, or the egress allowlist does not open the host.

fields.host: the git host the credential is for, github.com by default
fields.auth: token for an access token, github_app for a GitHub App
fields.token: a fine-grained access token with Contents: read, typed once
fields.app_id: the GitHub App's id, for auth github_app
fields.installation_id: the App's installation on the repository, optional
fields.private_key: the App's private key, typed once
fields.api_url: the GitHub API address, https://api.github.com by default (change it for GitHub Enterprise Server)

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A Microsoft Entra administrator who can **grant admin consent** (Global Administrator or Privileged
  Role Administrator).
- Someone who can **grant the app access to each site**: a SharePoint administrator, or a Graph caller
  holding `Sites.FullControl.All`. Consent alone opens no site (see Permissions).
- The address of each site to read, for example `https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Archi`.
- This is an organisation connector: an organisation administrator declares it once, and knowledge
  sources pick it by name.

sections.title: At Microsoft
sections.markdown:
1. Entra admin center, **App registrations**, **New registration**. Name it for the platform, single
   tenant, no redirect URI.
2. On the new app's Overview page, copy the **Directory (tenant) ID** and the **Application (client) ID**.
3. **Certificates & secrets**, **New client secret**. Copy the secret's **Value** now: it is shown once.
   The Value is what Choregos needs, not the Secret ID. A secret expires (24 months at most): note the
   date in your calendar, because the day it expires every sync of this connector fails.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
Least privilege first: the app reads only the sites you name.

1. **API permissions**, **Add a permission**, **Microsoft Graph**, **Application permissions**,
   `Sites.Selected`, then **Grant admin consent**. Never `Files.Read.All` or `Sites.Read.All`.
2. Grant the app **each site**. Find the site's id with
   `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/<host>:/sites/<path>` (the answer's `id`), then
   `POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/permissions` with the body
   `{"roles": ["read"], "grantedToIdentities": [{"application": {"id": "<client_id>", "displayName": "Choregos"}}]}`.
   The call must be made by a caller that holds `Sites.FullControl.All`. PnP PowerShell does the same
   with `Grant-PnPAzureADAppSitePermission -AppId <client_id> -DisplayName Choregos -Site <site url> -Permissions Read`.

Without step 2 the app is authorised and reads **nothing**: every site answers 403.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Documents**, type **SharePoint**, any name
   (it is lowercase, and knowledge sources refer to it).
2. `tenant_id`: the Directory (tenant) ID. `client_id`: the Application (client) ID.
3. `client_secret`: paste the secret's Value in the password field. It is sealed and never shown again;
   to rotate it, use **Replace**.
4. Leave `graph_url` and `login_url` alone unless you use a sovereign cloud.
5. Then **Knowledge**, a base, **Add source**, **SharePoint**: pick this connector, the site (or a
   OneDrive's drive) and, if you want, a folder.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
This connector has no test button of its own. Add the source, then press **Sync now**: the source shows
what it added and, if it failed, its last error. A first sync that lists documents proves the secret,
the consent and the site grant at once.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `AADSTS7000215` (invalid client secret): the Secret **ID** was pasted instead of the **Value**.
- `AADSTS700016` (application not found): wrong `client_id`, or wrong `tenant_id`.
- `403 accessDenied` on a site: the site grant (Permissions, step 2) is missing for that site.
- `401` months after it worked: the client secret expired. Create a new one and **Replace** it.
- A timeout: the API cannot reach `graph.microsoft.com` or `login.microsoftonline.com`; the
  network egress allowlist must open both.

fields.tenant_id: Directory (tenant) ID, from the app's Overview page
fields.client_id: Application (client) ID, from the app's Overview page
fields.client_secret: the secret's Value (not its Secret ID), typed once

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A pfSense with the **REST API package** (`pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI`, v2) installed, and an administrator who
  can create a user and an API key for it.
- Reads (rules, aliases, port forwards, interfaces, gateway status) are allowed operations. Writes
  (create, update, delete, restore a rule) are **governed actions**: they wait for a person's approval and
  carry a compensation that puts the previous rule back.
- The platform must be able to reach the firewall's management address from where the API runs.

sections.title: At pfSense
sections.markdown:
1. Create a dedicated user whose privileges are only the REST API pages the operations use.
2. Generate an **API key** for that user (the package's own settings; check its documentation at
   pfrest.org for the current menu).
3. Note the address (`https://<pfsense>`) and the CA that signed its certificate.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The key can do what its user's privileges allow, so give a read-only user if agents only need to read. Even
with write rights, no write happens without a human approval in Choregos.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Firewall**, type **pfSense**.
2. `base_url`: `https://<pfsense>`, **without** `/api/v2`.
3. `ca_cert`: the PEM of the CA, if the certificate is private. Keep `verify_tls` true:
   `verify_tls: false` is accepted in development only, logged each time, and refused in staging and prod.
4. `api_key`: in the password field. Then open the operations the agents need.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test** on the connector, then run `list_firewall_rules` or `gateway_status` from a workflow.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A TLS error: the certificate's CA is not trusted; set `ca_cert`.
- `401` or `403`: the API key is wrong, or its user lacks the privilege for that page.
- `404` on `/api/v2/...`: the REST API package is missing or is not v2, or `base_url` ends in `/api/v2`.
- A timeout: the platform cannot route to the management address.

fields.ca_cert: PEM of the CA that signed the device's certificate
fields.api_key: the REST API key of a pfSense user, typed once

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- **Development only.** This gateway hands out the key it was given: it mints no key per run, so there is
  no hard cap, and the cost ledger stays at zero. On staging and prod Choregos **refuses to build it** and
  says so: use `litellm` (or `openai-compatible`, knowing its limits).

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: Create a provider API key with a spending limit set at the provider's side.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: The key is used as is by every run. Give it only the models you list.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown: Connectors, **Gateway**, type **direct**: `models` (a list of names), `key` in the password field.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Run a stage on a development project.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A refusal that names `gateway: direct` in staging or prod: by design; change the gateway type.
- A cost always at zero: expected, nothing is measured.

fields.models: the model names the key may use

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A LiteLLM proxy and its **master key**. The platform uses it to **mint one virtual key per run**, with
  a hard budget: when the budget is reached LiteLLM refuses, and the run ends `failed (reason=budget)`.
- The usual place for this is the chart: `global.gateway.url` and `global.gateway.secretRef` (key
  `master-key`). A deployment-wide default needs no connector.
- Adding a model for agents to use is done at the gateway; the model catalogue of the administration
  lists what it routes.

sections.title: At LiteLLM
sections.markdown:
Create the models in the proxy's configuration. Optionally create a **team** and note its id so that spend
is attributed to it.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The master key can mint and revoke keys and read spend, so it is the platform's: the runner never holds it
(it gets a per-run key). Tags on keys are a LiteLLM **Enterprise** feature: on the open-source proxy leave
`enterprise_tags` false, or minting fails with `403`.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Chart values, or Connectors, **Gateway**, type **LiteLLM**: `base_url`, optionally `team_id`,
`internal_prices`, `enterprise_tags`, and `master_key` in the password field.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then open the administration's models list: it shows what the proxy routes.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401 LiteLLM Virtual Key expected. Received=<no value>`: the master key never resolved (a missing
  secret renders as the words `<no value>`); the API refuses to start in that case, so fix the secret's
  source.
- `403` when minting keys: `enterprise_tags` is on against an open-source proxy.
- No models listed: the proxy has none, or the key cannot list them.

fields.team_id: the LiteLLM team projects are attributed to
fields.internal_prices: a price list for models the proxy cannot price
fields.enterprise_tags: true only on LiteLLM Enterprise: key tags
fields.master_key: the proxy's master key, typed once

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- Any gateway that serves `GET {base_url}/models` and `/chat/completions` (Portkey, Kong AI Gateway, Envoy
  AI Gateway, OpenRouter, a vLLM router...).
- Read the limits first. This adapter gives **discovery only**: no per-run virtual key, no hard budget at
  the source, no measured cost (spend is "not measured", not "free"). Choregos alone holds the budget
  (the reservation, turns and minutes).

sections.title: At the gateway
sections.markdown:
Create two credentials: one for **discovery** (`api_key`), and one that **runs** will use (`run_key`). Every
run receives the same `run_key`, so scope it at the gateway: a consumer of its own, with its own token rate
limit.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
`api_key` only lists models. `run_key` can call the models you allow: that is where the damage is bounded,
so bound it there.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Chart (`global.gateway.type: openai-compatible`) or Connectors, **Gateway**: `base_url`, optional `headers`
and `timeout_s`, then `api_key` and `run_key` in their password fields.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Open the administration's models list: it shows what `GET {base_url}/models` returns.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- An empty models list: the `api_key` cannot list, or `base_url` is wrong (it must be the base of the API).
- `401`: wrong key, or a header the gateway needs is missing (`headers`).
- Spend always shows nothing: expected with this adapter.

fields.base_url: the gateway's address, ending where /models and /chat/completions hang
fields.api_key: the key used to discover models, typed once
fields.run_key: the key every run receives, typed once

title: Connect Microsoft Entra ID for joiners and leavers

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- An Entra administrator (Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator) who can grant consent
  and assign directory roles.
- An **administrative unit** that holds only the accounts the platform may manage. A
  restricted-management administrative unit is recommended.
- This connector writes to the directory: its operations (`create_user`, `add_to_group`,
  `remove_from_group`, `disable_user`, `revoke_sessions`) are governed actions that wait for a human
  approval, and `get_user` reads.

sections.title: At Microsoft
sections.markdown:
1. App registrations, **New registration** (single tenant, no redirect URI). Copy the **Directory
   (tenant) ID** and the **Application (client) ID**.
2. **Certificates & secrets**, **New client secret**: copy the **Value**, shown once. Note its expiry.
3. Create the administrative unit (Entra ID, Roles & admins, Administrative units) and copy its
   **Object ID**.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
Preferred, because it is bounded: give the app's service principal the **User Administrator** and
**Groups Administrator** roles **scoped to the administrative unit** (Roles and administrators, open the
role, **Add assignments**, choose the administrative unit scope, select the app).

Fallback: Microsoft Graph **application** permissions `User.ReadWrite.All` and `GroupMember.ReadWrite.All`
with admin consent. They are **tenant-wide**: the connector refuses to touch an account outside
`administrative_unit_id`, and that check is then the only bound. Say so when you ask for approval.

Not proven here: the role-based variant has not been run against a live tenant from this repository.
Check the first run on a test unit before pointing it at people.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Identity**, type **Microsoft Entra ID**.
2. `tenant_id`, `client_id`: from the app's Overview. `client_secret`: the Value, in the password field.
3. `administrative_unit_id`: the unit's Object ID. Every account the platform creates enters it; any
   other account is refused.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Run a workflow step (or ask through the MCP door) that calls `get_user` on a known user principal name
inside the unit. A returned profile proves the secret and the read permission.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `AADSTS7000215`: the Secret ID was pasted instead of the Value.
- `AADSTS700016`: wrong `client_id` or `tenant_id`.
- `403 Authorization_RequestDenied`: the role or permission is missing, or the target account is not in
  the administrative unit.
- A refusal naming the administrative unit: the account is outside `administrative_unit_id`, by design.
- A timeout: open `graph.microsoft.com` and `login.microsoftonline.com` in the egress allowlist.

fields.administrative_unit_id: the Object ID of the administrative unit the platform may touch

- A free Alpha Vantage API key. The free tier allows about **25 requests a day** and gives **unadjusted**

sections.title: At the vendor

sections.markdown: The key only reads market data. It is yours: do not share one key between organisations.

sections.title: Test it

sections.title: When it fails

- A note about the call frequency or "standard API call frequency": the daily limit is reached; wait or
  upgrade.
- An invalid key message: the key is wrong or not activated.
- Prices that look off after a split: the bars are unadjusted.

title: Combine several market data sources

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- Decide which sources to combine: `stooq`, `yahoo` and `alphavantage`. Each has its own limits and terms:
  see their procedures. The composite tries them **in order** and falls back to the next when one fails.
- With `cross_check` on, the closes of two sources are compared and a difference above `tolerance` (2 % by
  default) is reported, which catches a broken or unadjusted source.

sections.title: At the vendors
sections.markdown: Only what each source needs: nothing for Stooq and Yahoo, an API key for Alpha Vantage.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: They read public market data. Nothing is written.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Connectors, **Market data**, type **composite**. `sources`: for example `["stooq", "alphavantage"]`.
`source_configs`: a sub-configuration per provider, for example `{"stooq": {"suffix_map": {}}}`.
`cross_check` and `tolerance`. Keys in their password fields: `stooq_api_key`, `alphavantage_api_key`.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then call `get_bars` and compare with a source you trust.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A disagreement reported between sources: one is unadjusted (Alpha Vantage free), or a corporate action
  happened; check the dates before trusting either.
- Everything falls back to the last source: the first ones fail; see their procedures.
- A rate limit: the free tiers are small; order the sources so the limited one is last.

egress: the hosts of the sources it combines

fields.sources: the providers, in the order they are tried: stooq, yahoo, alphavantage
fields.source_configs: the configuration of each provider, by name
fields.cross_check: true to compare the closes of two sources
fields.tolerance: the largest relative difference of two closes before they disagree, 0.02 by default
fields.stooq_api_key: Stooq's key, if any, typed once

title: Use Stooq for daily market data

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- Stooq serves **daily** bars as CSV, free. Read Stooq's terms of use before relying on it.
- It is the right default for a study or a backtest on daily closes; it is not a real-time feed.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown:
Stooq may demand an `apikey` on CSV downloads, obtained once through its site. Without one, the endpoint can
answer a "get your apikey" page instead of data. Get the key there and put it in `api_key`.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: None: it only reads public market data. Nothing is written.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Connectors, **Market data**, type **Stooq**. `suffix_map` maps your tickers to Stooq's market suffixes
(for example the empty suffix to `.us`, `.L` to `.uk`). `timeout_s` defaults to 20.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then call `get_instrument` and `get_bars` for a known ticker.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A "get your apikey" answer: set `api_key`.
- No bars: the ticker's suffix is not in `suffix_map`, so Stooq does not know the symbol.
- Empty or truncated data: the market was closed, or the date range has no sessions.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `stooq.com`.

fields.suffix_map: ticker suffix to Stooq market suffix, for example {"": ".us", ".L": ".uk"}

title: Use Yahoo Finance for daily market data

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- This uses Yahoo Finance's **unofficial** chart endpoint. It is for personal use, and it **may break** or be
  blocked without notice. Read Yahoo's terms of service before using it for anything else.
- Prefer a source with a stated licence for anything that matters; the `composite` type can cross-check it
  against another.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: Nothing to create: there is no key.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: None: it reads public data.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown: Connectors, **Market data**, type **Yahoo**. The only option is `timeout_s` (20 by default).

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then call `get_bars` for a known ticker.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- Empty answers or `429`: Yahoo is throttling or blocking the platform's address.
- A changed format: the endpoint is unofficial and may have changed; use another source.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `query1.finance.yahoo.com`.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- The server's **Streamable HTTP** endpoint, over https. A server that speaks only the older SSE
  transport is refused.
- An organisation administrator declares the connector. What an agent may then call is decided tool by
  tool, below.
- Read the vendor's terms: the server acts with the token's account, and everything an agent sends to
  it leaves the platform.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown:
Create the credential in the vendor's own settings: an API token, a service account key, or a personal
access token. The catalogue entry for a known server says where. Prefer a token of a dedicated account
whose rights are exactly what the agents should have, and the narrowest scopes the vendor offers.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- The connector's tools act with **that account's permissions**, nothing in Choregos can widen them.
- Tools are **born closed**: after discovery each tool is `forbidden` until an administrator
  opens it. A read can be `allowed`; a write is a governed action that waits for approval.
- A project sees only the tools its groups are opened to, and can only tighten them.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **MCP**, type **MCP server**, a lowercase name.
2. `url`: the endpoint.
3. `auth_scheme`: `bearer` (the default) sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `basic` sends
   `Authorization: Basic base64(username:token)`; it needs `username`, usually an email.
4. `token`: paste it in the password field. It is sealed and shown once; **Replace** rotates it.
5. Press **Discover**, then open the operations the agents need, one by one.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: **Discover** asks the server for its tools. A list of tools proves the URL, the scheme and the token.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401` or `403`: the token is wrong, expired, or sent with the wrong scheme (Bearer versus Basic).
- `406 Not Acceptable`: the server wants an `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` header and
  rejected the request; check that the URL is the Streamable HTTP endpoint and not an SSE one.
- A timeout or a connection refused: the egress allowlist does not open the server's host.
- "No tools", or only a few: discovery has not run, or the token's scopes are too narrow for the server
  to list more.

fields.url: the server's Streamable HTTP endpoint, https
fields.token: the token or key the vendor gave you, typed once

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- An Atlassian organisation administrator, because **API token access to the Rovo MCP Server is off
  until an admin enables it**.
- This gives agents Atlassian's tools (search, Jira, Confluence, and more) under Choregos's per-tool
  policy. It does not call the Rovo agent itself; for that, see the remote agent procedure.
- The server allows about 1 000 calls an hour on Standard and Premium plans.

sections.title: At Atlassian
sections.markdown:
1. Atlassian Administration: enable **API token authentication** for the Rovo MCP Server.
2. Create the credential. Two kinds exist and they are sent differently:
   - a **personal API token with scopes** (id.atlassian.com, Security, API tokens), sent as **Basic**
     with the account's email;
   - a **service account API key** (Directory, Service accounts), sent as **Bearer**.
3. The server's endpoint is `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp`. The older `/v1/sse` endpoint stopped on
   30 June 2026. The MCP server catalogue may list a newer `/v2/mcp` address that signs in with OAuth
   instead: this procedure is the API-token route on `/v1/mcp`; check Atlassian's documentation for the
   address your site supports.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- Give the token granular scopes. A starting set for reading: `read:jira-work`, `read:page:confluence`,
  `search:confluence`, `search:rovo:mcp`. Add `write:jira-work` and the like only if agents must write.
- With classic or broad scopes, only the **Teamwork Graph** tools appear (Atlassian's own knowledge-base
  article says so). If you see only those, the token is the cause.
- Every tool acts with the account's own Jira and Confluence permissions.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Install it from the MCP catalogue ("Atlassian Rovo MCP"), or Administration, **Connectors**,
   **Declare**: capability **MCP**, type **MCP server**.
2. `url`: `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp`.
3. Personal token: `auth_scheme` `basic`, `username` the account's email. Service account key:
   `auth_scheme` `bearer`. A personal token sent as Bearer fails.
4. `token`: the token or key, in the password field.
5. **Discover**, then open the tools the agents need.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Discover**. The list should include Jira and Confluence tools, not only Teamwork Graph ones.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `401`: wrong scheme for the credential (a personal token needs `basic`, a service account key
  needs `bearer`), a wrong email, or API token access is not enabled by an administrator.
- Only a few Teamwork Graph tools: the token's scopes are classic or too broad; create a token with
  granular scopes.
- `429`: the hourly limit.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `mcp.atlassian.com`.

fields.auth_scheme: basic for a personal API token, bearer for a service account API key
fields.token: the API token or key, typed once

vendor_docs.title: Configuring authentication via API token (Rovo MCP Server)
Rovo MCP Server only returns Teamwork Graph tools when using an API token
Manage API tokens for service accounts

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
This is a **demonstration** of the device management (laptops, phones): it is held in memory and is **refused in staging and prod**. Use it
to try the joiners-leavers and delivery templates without any real system.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: There is no vendor. Nothing is created anywhere.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: None: nothing leaves the platform. Nothing is stored beyond the process's memory, so it forgets on restart.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Declare the connector with type `demo`. Leave `url` empty to run the fakes in the same process, or give
the address of the one process that serves them for several replicas.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Run the template's workflow. The demonstration answers like the real system would, with invented data.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A refusal in staging or prod: by design. Declare the real connector instead.
- State that disappears: it lives in memory; with several replicas, set `url` to a single process.

fields.url: the endpoint of the one process serving the demonstration fakes; empty to run them in this process
fields.api_key: not needed by the demonstration, typed once if you set one

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A running Ecphoria. The chart can deploy one (`global.memory.embedded: true`) or point at yours
  (`global.memory.url`, `global.memory.tokenSecret`).
- Memory is optional: without it the platform falls back to the `lexical` memory, with no service.
- Reads have a short timeout on purpose (300 ms by default): a slow memory never blocks a stage, it gives
  an empty context pack. Writes are governed: the orchestrator writes, the agent proposes.

sections.title: At Ecphoria
sections.markdown:
Create or choose the **tenant** each project writes to, and a token if Ecphoria requires one. Ecphoria's
own documentation is the reference for that; this repository does not describe it.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The token must be able to read and write memories of the tenant and create tenants if the platform is to
create one per project.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Usually the chart's `global.memory.*` values. To declare it on a project: Connectors, **Memory**, type
**Ecphoria**, `base_url`, `tenant`, optionally `read_timeout_ms`, and `token` in the password field.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**: it calls Ecphoria's `/health` for the tenant and shows its status.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `ok: false` with an error: the address is unreachable from the API, or the token is refused.
- Runs start with an empty memory: the read hit the timeout; raise `read_timeout_ms` if Ecphoria is
  healthy but slow.
- `401` on writes: the token lacks write rights.

fields.tenant: the Ecphoria tenant a project writes to
fields.read_timeout_ms: how long a read may take before the run goes on without memory

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
Nothing to install. The lexical memory is the fallback: it searches by words in the platform's own
database, with no external service and no embedding.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: There is no vendor and nothing to create.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: It reads and writes only the platform's own tables, under the organisation's isolation.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown: Connectors, **Memory**, type **lexical**. There is nothing to configure.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then run a stage and look at its context pack.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown: - Poor recall on paraphrases: it matches words, not meaning. Use Ecphoria for semantic memory.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
This name is **deprecated** and is never offered to a new project. It is kept so projects that already
carry it keep working. It is an alias of the `lexical` memory: the name promised vectors, the code does
full-text search.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: Nothing to create.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: Same as the lexical memory: the platform's own tables only.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown: Change the project's memory connector to `lexical` (same behaviour) or `ecphoria` (semantic memory).

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test** on the new connector and run a stage.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown: - A project that still names `pgvector` works as `lexical`; if you expected vectors, switch to Ecphoria.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A cluster running Cilium, with **Hubble Relay** if you want flows. The platform reads policies from the
  Kubernetes API and flows through the `hubble` CLI against Relay (the CLI ships in the API and worker
  image, never in the runner).
- A GitOps repository where policy changes are proposed as pull requests. **No path applies a policy to a
  cluster**: a change is a pull request that your release process carries.

sections.title: At the cluster
sections.markdown:
1. A dedicated **read-only service account**, never the pod's own token, with a `ClusterRole` that can
   `get` and `list` `ciliumnetworkpolicies` and `ciliumclusterwidenetworkpolicies` (`cilium.io`), and a
   binding. Create a token for it.
2. If Hubble Relay requires mTLS, issue a client certificate and key for the platform.
3. A token for the GitOps repository that can push a branch and open a pull request.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- Kubernetes: `get` and `list` on the two Cilium policy kinds, nothing else.
- Relay: read of flows.
- GitOps repository: branch and pull request only. The platform never merges it.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Network policy**, type **Cilium**.
2. `kubernetes_url`, `ca_cert`, and `token` (password field). `verify_tls` stays true; `false` is for
   development only.
3. For flows: `hubble_server`, `hubble_tls`, `hubble_ca_cert`, `hubble_tls_server_name`, and for mTLS
   `hubble_client_cert` and `hubble_client_key`.
4. For proposals: `gitops_repo`, `gitops_base` (default `main`), `gitops_path` (default `cilium`) and
   `gitops_token`.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Press **Test**, then call `list_network_policies` and `get_flows` from a workflow.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `Forbidden` from the API server: the role is missing or not bound to the account.
- A TLS error: set `ca_cert` (cluster) or `hubble_ca_cert` (Relay).
- No flows: Relay is not reachable, or requires mTLS you did not configure.
- A proposal that fails: `gitops_token` cannot push to `gitops_repo`.

fields.token: the read-only service account's token, typed once
fields.hubble_server: Hubble Relay's address, hubble-relay.kube-system.svc:443 by default
fields.hubble_client_key: the mTLS client key, if Relay requires one
fields.gitops_repo: owner/repo where policy changes are proposed
fields.gitops_token: a token that can open a pull request there, typed once

title: Connect Slack for notifications and decisions

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A Slack workspace where you may create or install an app (otherwise an administrator does).
- The channel notifications go to.
- Choose a mode. **Incoming webhook**: simplest, fixed to one channel. **Bot token**: posts to any
  channel the bot is in, and can also be tested with `auth.test`.

sections.title: At Slack
sections.markdown:
1. `api.slack.com/apps`, **Create New App**, **From scratch**, pick the workspace.
2. Either:
   - **Incoming Webhooks**: turn it on, **Add New Webhook to Workspace**, pick the channel, copy the
     webhook URL; or
   - **OAuth & Permissions**: add the bot scope `chat:write` (and `chat:write.public` to post in
     channels the bot has not joined), **Install to Workspace**, copy the **Bot User OAuth Token**.
3. For a bot token, invite the bot to the channel: `/invite @<app name>`.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
- Webhook mode needs nothing else: the webhook can post to the one channel you picked.
- Bot mode needs `chat:write`. Nothing else is read from the workspace.
- Do not enable Interactivity: Choregos exposes no Slack interactivity endpoint today, so a message's
  decision buttons do not post back. The button that opens the item in the console is a plain link and
  works; decisions are taken in the console.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Project settings, Connectors, **Notify**, type **Slack** (or an organisation connector).
2. `channel`: for example `#choregos`.
3. `public_url`: this platform's console address, `https://choregos.example.com`. Messages carry a button that opens
   the item here.
4. Paste **one** of `webhook_url` or `bot_token` in its password field (sealed, shown once).

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Press **Test** on the connector. In bot mode it calls `auth.test` and shows the workspace; in webhook
mode it checks that a webhook URL is set. Then trigger a notification and look at the channel.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `channel_not_found`: the channel name is wrong, or the bot cannot see a private channel.
- `not_in_channel`: invite the bot (`/invite @app`), or add `chat:write.public`.
- `invalid_auth` or `token_revoked`: the bot token is wrong or the app was reinstalled; paste the new one.
- A `404` or `no_service` from a webhook: the webhook was revoked; create a new one.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `slack.com` (bot) or `hooks.slack.com` (webhook).

fields.channel: the channel notifications go to, for example #choregos
fields.public_url: this platform's console address, used for the buttons' links
fields.bot_token: a bot token (the mode that posts to any channel it is in)

title: Run agent stages as Azure Container Apps jobs

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- An Azure subscription, a resource group and a **Container Apps environment**, and a registry that holds
  the runner image.
- A **user-assigned managed identity** with pull rights on the registry: the job pulls its image with it,
  so no cloud credential is held by the runner.
- See the deployment guide and the `github-aca` template.

sections.title: At Azure
sections.markdown:
1. Create an app registration (service principal) for the platform and a client secret; note the tenant
   id, client id and the secret's **Value**.
2. Give it a role that can create and start jobs in the resource group (for example a custom role on
   `Microsoft.App/jobs/*`; check Azure's built-in roles for the narrowest that fits).
3. Note the environment's resource id, the managed identity's resource id and the registry host.
4. Optional: a Log Analytics workspace, so the platform can read the job's logs. Without it, logs say
   where to look instead of showing nothing.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The service principal creates and starts jobs; the managed identity only pulls images. The run's token is
a job secret referenced by `secretRef`, never an environment variable in clear.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Set `runner.executor: aca` in the chart and declare the connector: `subscription_id`, `resource_group`,
`environment_id` (required), `location` (default `westeurope`), `tenant_id`, `client_id`, `client_secret`
(password field; or a ready `token` instead of the three identity fields), `identity_id`, `registry_server` and `log_analytics_workspace_id`.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Start a run on a test project: the job appears in the resource group and its execution finishes.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `AuthorizationFailed`: the service principal's role does not cover the resource group.
- The job cannot pull its image: the managed identity lacks pull rights on the registry.
- No logs: no Log Analytics workspace is configured.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist must open `management.azure.com` and `login.microsoftonline.com`.

fields.resource_group: the resource group of the jobs
fields.environment_id: the Container Apps environment's resource id
fields.client_secret: the service principal's secret, typed once
fields.token: an Azure Resource Manager access token you already hold, instead of tenant_id, client_id and client_secret
fields.identity_id: the managed identity the job uses to pull its image
fields.log_analytics_workspace_id: where the job's logs are read

title: Run agent stages in warm sandboxes (opt-in)

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- The agent-sandbox **operator**, whose CRDs are cluster-scoped: a platform team installs it, a tenant of
  a shared cluster cannot. `tekton` and `k8s_job` stay the defaults.
- Read the deployment guide, section "The `agent_sandbox` executor": it is the reference;
  this page is its checklist.

sections.title: At the cluster
sections.markdown:
1. The operator, pinned (v1.0.6 at the time of writing), by Argo CD or by hand with
   `kubectl apply --server-side -k infra/operators/agent-sandbox`.
2. The Kyverno policy of the repository so a template that breaks non-root is refused where it is written.
3. The chart: `runner.executor: agent_sandbox`, `runner.namespacePattern` set to the release namespace,
   `runner.warmPool.size`, `runner.runtimeClass`, `runner.sandbox.*`.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
`global.rbac.jobRunner: true`, or the platform grants the same verbs. The chart renders a NetworkPolicy
so only the orchestrator's workers reach the assignment port; where the platform forbids a tenant's
NetworkPolicy, set `runner.sandbox.assignmentNetworkPolicy: false` and close that port yourself.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Chart values; the connector's `pool_image`, `max_active` and the rest are optional. A step that names its
own image is refused in a pool: use `k8s_job` for such steps.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
`CHOREGOS_CLUSTER_CONTEXT=<context> CHOREGOS_CLUSTER_ALLOW_SHARED=<context> make test-cluster` on a
cluster that has the operator (it uses a namespace of its own and deletes it).

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A claim that never binds: the pool is empty and the template cannot cold-start; check the operator.
- A refusal about a RuntimeClass or an image: the pool was made with another one; recreate it.
- A run that waits: `max_active` is reached; it is admitted in arrival order.

fields.warm_pool: the SandboxWarmPool's name, choregos-runner by default
fields.pool_image: the image the pool's pods are made from
fields.runtime_class: the template's RuntimeClass, for example gvisor
fields.max_active: concurrent runs; beyond it a run waits

title: Run agent stages as Kubernetes Jobs

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A Kubernetes cluster and a namespace for agent pods. This is the executor with the fewest moving parts
  and the one that supports queueing; use it when Tekton is not there.
- This is a chart setting, not a form: `runner.executor: k8s_job` in the orchestrator's values.

sections.title: At the cluster
sections.markdown:
Set the values of `choregos-orchestrator.runner` (see the deployment guide, "Running agent stages"):
`executor`, `namespacePattern` (for example `proj-{slug}-runners`), `maxActive`, `limits`, and
`envFromSecrets` for credentials mounted by reference into each agent pod.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The orchestrator needs rights to create and read `Job`s and `Secret`s in the runner namespaces
(`global.rbac.jobRunner: true`, or the platform grants the same verbs). Under a namespace `LimitRange`,
set `runner.limits` below the per-container ceiling, or the pod is rejected and the Job waits without
saying why.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Nothing to type: the executor is chosen by the chart. `maxActive` caps concurrent runs per namespace;
beyond it a Job is created suspended (no pod, no image pull, no quota) and admitted in arrival order.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Start a run on a test project and watch its pod: `kubectl get jobs -n <runner namespace>`.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A Job that never starts: the namespace quota or a `LimitRange` refuses the pod. Lower `runner.limits`.
- `Forbidden` creating the Job: the orchestrator's service account lacks the rights above.
- A pod that cannot pull its image: the image or registry credentials; the run reports the container's
  reason and the runner's exit code.

title: Run agent stages in local Docker (development)

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- Development only: it needs a Docker daemon on the machine that runs the orchestrator.
- Use it with `docker compose up` (`dev/compose.yaml`). On a cluster use `k8s_job` or `tekton`.

sections.title: At the host
sections.markdown:
Docker must be installed and the orchestrator must be able to call it. The runner image is pulled on the
first run, which can take several minutes (the pull has a 15 minute timeout).

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: Whoever can reach the Docker socket controls the host. Do not use this executor on a shared machine.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Chart or compose settings: `runner.executor: local_docker`. The only option is `network`, the Docker
network the runner container joins so it can reach the API.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Start a run: `docker ps` shows a container named `choregos-run-<id>`.

A finished run keeps its container, so `docker logs choregos-run-<id>` still works. The ten newest
finished containers are kept; older ones are removed when the next run starts.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- The run cannot reach the API: the container is not on `network`.
- `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon`: the orchestrator has no access to the socket.
- A very slow first run: the runner image is still being pulled.

fields.network: the Docker network the runner joins, choregos_default by default

title: Run agent stages as Tekton PipelineRuns

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A cluster with Tekton Pipelines, and a `Pipeline` named `choregos-agent` (or your own name) in the
  runner namespace, installed from the chart.
- The default executor when Tekton is present: `runner.executor: tekton`.

sections.title: At the cluster
sections.markdown:
Install Tekton, then the chart's Pipeline. Set `runner.executor: tekton` and `runner.namespacePattern`
in the orchestrator's values. Each agent stage becomes one `PipelineRun`; its Secret belongs to the run
and goes with it however it ends.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
The orchestrator creates, reads and deletes `PipelineRun`s and `Secret`s in the runner namespaces. The
`service_account` is the identity of the stage's pod: give it nothing beyond what the runner needs.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
Mostly chart values. If a connector is declared, `pipeline` names the Pipeline to start and
`service_account` the account it runs as.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown: Start a run and look at `kubectl get pipelineruns -n <runner namespace>`.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- A `PipelineRun` that never schedules: the Pipeline name does not exist in that namespace.
- `Forbidden`: the orchestrator's service account lacks `pipelineruns` rights.
- The run's pod is rejected at admission: see the namespace policies (security context, `LimitRange`).

fields.pipeline: the Pipeline each run starts, choregos-agent by default
fields.service_account: the service account the PipelineRun runs as

title: Use GitHub for branches, pull requests and checks

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- The same **GitHub App** as the tracker (see "Use GitHub Issues and Projects v2 as the board"): one App
  serves both. Its id, private key and webhook secret are platform settings.
- The repository the agents change. They work on a branch and open a pull request; nothing is pushed to
  the default branch.

sections.title: At GitHub
sections.markdown:
1. Create the App with the **Webhook URL** `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/github`, or reuse the platform's.
2. **Install** it on the repository: the repository field's **Install on GitHub** button opens GitHub's
   install page and brings you back. The installation is discovered by the platform: there
   is no number to copy.
3. For `merge_queue`, enable a **merge queue** in the repository's branch protection (Settings, Branches).
   Without one, set `merge_queue` to false.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown:
Repository permissions:

- `contents`: write
- `issues`: write
- `pull_requests`: write
- `checks`: write
- `metadata`: read

Organization permissions, only if the same App serves the Projects v2 board:

- `organization_projects`: write

Subscribe to these events: `issues`, `issue_comment`, `projects_v2_item`, `pull_request`, `pull_request_review`, `check_suite`, `check_run`.

Add `workflows: write` only if agents edit `.github/workflows`.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Project settings, Connectors, **SCM**, type **GitHub (App)**.
2. `repo`: pick the repository in the list (what the App's installations claimed by your organisation
   see), or type `owner/repo` when the list cannot be read.
3. `merge_queue`: true (the default) enqueues through the merge queue; `merge_method`: `SQUASH` (the
   default), `MERGE` or `REBASE`.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Press **Test**: it reads the repository through the App. A run that opens a pull request then proves
the write permissions.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- `404` on the repository, or the repository missing from the list: the App is not installed on it, or
  its installation is not claimed by your organisation. Press **Install on GitHub**, or **Refresh**.
- `403` on a branch, a pull request or a check: a permission above is missing or its upgrade was not
  accepted on the installation.
- A merge that never happens: the merge queue is not enabled on the branch, or a required check is red.
- A push refused for a workflow file: the App lacks `workflows: write`.

sections.title: At GitHub

1. Organization settings, Developer settings, **GitHub Apps**, **New GitHub App**.
2. **Webhook URL**: `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/github`. **Webhook secret**: a random string, the same one the

- `contents`: write
- `issues`: write
- `pull_requests`: write
- `checks`: write
- `metadata`: read

- `organization_projects`: write

Subscribe to these events: `issues`, `issue_comment`, `projects_v2_item`, `pull_request`, `pull_request_review`, `check_suite`, `check_run`.

refuses such a push.

sections.title: In Choregos

   see), or type `owner/repo` when the list cannot be read.
3. For a board: `org` and `project_number` (the number in the board's address).

  its installation is not claimed by your organisation. Press **Install on GitHub** (or add the
  repository to the installation), then **Refresh**.

  installation (GitHub asks the owner to approve a change).

  `github-webhook-secret`.

  platform's and reachable from GitHub.

sections.markdown:

- The platform's shared webhook secret (`CHOREGOS_GENERIC_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), held by whoever operates
  Choregos. Jira Cloud does not sign webhooks, so the platform accepts a delivery only if it carries this
  secret in an `X-Choregos-Secret` header.

sections.markdown:
1. As the dedicated account: `id.atlassian.com`, Security, **API tokens**, **Create API token**. Copy the
   token when it is shown.
2. In the Jira project, give that account the permissions below.
3. **Webhook.** The endpoint is `https://choregos.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/jira` and it requires the header `X-Choregos-Secret`.

   added in the project, action **Send web request** to that URL with a custom header
   `X-Choregos-Secret`. This path has not been exercised against a live site from this repository.

On the project, for the dedicated account: **Browse projects**, **Create issues**, **Edit issues**,
**Transition issues**, **Add comments**.

`https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/<cloudId>` as the `base_url`; that variant is **not proven** here, so

3. `field_names`: only if your Jira names the custom fields Choregos writes differently. They are
   `Cost (€)`, `Size`, `Risk` and `Run`.

- A webhook answered `401 invalid shared secret`: the `X-Choregos-Secret` header is missing or differs
  from the platform's shared secret.

  this platform from Jira.

title: Search the web through Brave Search API

sections.title: Before you start
sections.markdown:
- A Brave Search API subscription and its key. Read the plan's terms on query retention before you
  fill `data_handling`.
- The built-in `web_search` returns links and snippets, never pages.

sections.title: At the vendor
sections.markdown: Create a key in the Brave Search API dashboard.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.markdown: The key only searches. It stays in the API: no runner ever sees it.

sections.title: In Choregos
sections.markdown:
1. Connectors, **Web search**, type **Brave Search API**. `api_key` in the password field (sealed, shown once).
2. Choregos does **not** know what Brave Search API keeps of a query: its terms were not reviewed. Under a
   ceiling that caps retention or forbids reuse, the tool stays off until you fill `data_handling` from
   your contract, for example `{"query_retention_days": 0, "query_reuse": false, "terms_ref": "contract
   ref, section"}`. A declaration can only be stricter, and `terms_ref` is required.
3. The organisation's ceiling opens the tool: Settings, **Policy ceiling**, `web_search: {mode: allow}`.

sections.title: Test it
sections.markdown:
Press **Test**, then start a run: the agent's tool list shows `web_search`. Each query writes a ledger
row `search:brave` and an event with the query's fingerprint, never its text.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- The tool is not offered: the ceiling is closed, the backend is not in its `backends`, or the declared
  data handling does not meet its bounds (an unknown value fails every bound that reads it).
- `query_redacted`: the query held what looks like a secret; nothing was sent.
- `rate_limited`: `requests_per_minute`, or Brave Search API's own quota, is reached; the answer says when to retry.
- `network_policy`: the organisation's network ceiling refuses `api.search.brave.com`.

fields.requests_per_minute: the organisation's queries per minute to this backend; beyond, the agent gets a 429
fields.data_handling: what your contract grants (retention, reuse, region) with its reference in terms_ref

  runner on the agent's workspace; files that exist only on the server, such as certificates, are
  reported as missing: the report is shown, not hidden.

Create a token (a fine-grained personal access token on the repository, or a GitHub App's) that can read
contents and open pull requests there.

sections.title: Permissions

1. Administration, **Connectors**, **Declare**: capability **Web server**, type **nginx**.

Nothing more than the connector's setup. To read a **sub-space**, open the branch's root page: its number
is in the address, `…/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/<id>/Title`.

sections.markdown:

the chosen tree or restricted against the account leaves the base at the next sync.

sections.title: When it fails
sections.markdown:
- "resolves to a private address": not crawled, by design.
- Nothing indexed: `robots.txt` disallows the paths, or the start page links nowhere under its path.
- A redirect to another host: the crawl does not follow it, and the base is not emptied.
- A timeout: the egress allowlist does not open the site.

fields.url: the https address the crawl starts from
fields.max_depth: how many links deep to follow, at most 5
fields.max_pages: how many pages to read, at most 500
fields.exclude: path globs, each starting with /, that are neither fetched nor followed
fields.include_documents: also read the PDF, Word, PowerPoint and Excel files the pages link to (same host)
